name: Resisoft
tagline: A small Uruguayan software outfit selling a managed line-of-business system to local operators.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This is the regional vertical software pattern: a local vendor, a Spanish-language site, no public price list, and a customer base that bought the vendor as much as the product. The screens themselves are boring CRUD, clients, items, documents, payments, reports, and an agent will happily generate all of it in an afternoon. What the agent cannot generate is conformance with Uruguayan invoicing and tax rules, the migration of years of existing records, or a human in the same time zone who answers the phone when month-end breaks. A personal replacement also makes little sense here, since nobody uses this kind of system personally; it is the back office of an actual business. Detail is thin on exactly which vertical this serves, so treat the specifics as unverified and the shape as typical.
coreLoopDIY: A local SQLite app that tracks clients, line items, documents and payments, and prints a PDF that is not a legally valid fiscal receipt.
requirements: A machine you are willing to be the only backup of
whatYouLose: Electronic invoicing that the tax authority actually accepts
Migration of existing records from the current system
Someone local who answers the phone when billing breaks on the 30th
Multi-user access, roles, and an audit trail your accountant trusts
Any liability sitting anywhere other than with you
moatNotes: Local fiscal rules plus a vendor the owner already trusts beats a better UI every single time in this segment.
whyPeopleStillPay: Businesses in this bracket are not paying for software, they are paying to not think about invoicing rules, to have their old data show up in the new system, and to have a named person to call. The engineering surface is small and the obligation surface is large, which is exactly the inverse of what a one-shot build is good at. Swapping it out means re-entering history, retraining staff, and owning every compliance edge case yourself, for a saving that is probably less than one afternoon of an accountant's time.
notes: The CRUD is a weekend; the tax authority is not. The moat is local fiscal compliance plus a phone number that a real business owner already trusts.
prompt:
Build a local-first back-office tracker for one small business. Nothing hosted, nothing multi-tenant.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15, App Router, TypeScript
- SQLite through better-sqlite3, file at ./data/app.db
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Server Actions for all mutations, no separate API layer
- pdf-lib for document output

Data model:
- clients: name, tax id, email, phone, address, notes
- items: name, description, unit price, tax rate
- documents: type (quote or invoice), client, issue date, due date, status (draft, sent, paid, void), line items with quantity and unit price snapshot
- payments: document, date, amount, method

Screens:
- Dashboard: outstanding total, overdue list, last 10 documents
- Clients list and detail with document history
- Items CRUD
- Document editor with live subtotal, tax and total
- Payments recorded against a document, with partial payments supported
- Reports page: revenue by month, revenue by client, CSV export of everything

Rules:
- Totals computed server side, stored in cents as integers, never floats
- Document numbers sequential per type, gapless, assigned on first send
- Seed script with 5 clients, 10 items and 20 documents so the UI is not empty

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt:
- Electronic fiscal invoicing or any tax authority integration
- Auth, users, roles, multi-tenancy
- Email sending, payment processors, cloud storage

Print a clear README line stating that generated PDFs are internal documents only and are not valid fiscal receipts. Any secrets go in .env.example, none hardcoded.
